findings.claim: You will sometimes be given a Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient and asked to interpret it in context.
findings.problem: Tier error against the Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 specification: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (both its calculation and its interpretation) is Higher-tier-only content. It is presented here in the main, untiered body of the lesson (and the Worked Example on interpreting a coefficient of -0.82 is likewise untiered), so Foundation students are taught it as assessed material they will not meet. Only the PMCC paragraph is correctly marked Higher.
findings.correction: Move the whole 'Interpreting Given Correlation Coefficients' section, including the worked example on the -0.82 coefficient, inside a <div class="higher-only"> block and head it 'Interpreting Given Correlation Coefficients (Higher)', opening: 'At Higher tier you may be given a Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient and asked to interpret it in context.'

findings.claim: {"q": "What range of values can Spearman's rank correlation coefficient take?", "a": "Between -1 and +1."} and {"q": "What does a Spearman's rank coefficient close to +1 indicate?", "a": "A strong positive correlation."}
findings.problem: Same tier error as the body text: Spearman's rank is Higher-tier-only content in Edexcel 1ST0, but these two cards are untagged while the PMCC cards carry '(Higher)'. Foundation candidates revising these cards spend time on out-of-tier material.
findings.correction: {"q": "What range of values can Spearman's rank correlation coefficient take? (Higher)", "a": "Between -1 and +1."} and {"q": "What does a Spearman's rank coefficient close to +1 indicate? (Higher)", "a": "A strong positive correlation."}

findings.claim: This loses marks even if the correlation is genuinely strong, because strength of correlation says nothing about cause. ... Using “associated with” instead of “causes” shows the examiner you understand the distinction.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertions about examiner behaviour and mark loss. No Edexcel 1ST0 specification or published mark scheme statement is supplied that says marks are deducted for the word 'causes' or that particular wording signals understanding to an examiner.
findings.correction: A statistically incorrect claim, because strength of correlation says nothing about cause. ... Writing “associated with” rather than “causes” keeps your answer statistically accurate.

findings.claim: a vague “correlation does not equal causation” with no named lurking variable rarely earns full marks
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner marking behaviour; the Edexcel 1ST0 specification makes no such statement and no published board document is cited.
findings.correction: naming a specific lurking variable makes your answer fuller and more clearly statistical than a bare “correlation does not equal causation”.

findings.claim: {"q": "What does Edexcel say can happen with lurking variables in complex situations? (Higher)", "a": "Multiple factors may interact to affect both variables."}
findings.problem: The card attributes a form of words to the awarding body. The Edexcel 1ST0 specification is not quoted as saying this, so the attribution is unevidenced; the statistical point itself is sound and should be asked without the attribution.
findings.correction: {"q": "In a complex real situation, why may naming one lurking variable be incomplete? (Higher)", "a": "Several factors can interact, together affecting both variables and producing the apparent correlation."}

findings.claim: spurious correlation: A correlation between two variables that arises not because one causes the other, but because both are influenced by a third, shared factor.
findings.problem: Over-narrow definition. A spurious correlation is any correlation between variables with no causal link between them; it may arise from a third (lurking) variable or purely by coincidence. Restricting it to the third-variable case excludes the coincidental case candidates are also expected to recognise.
findings.correction: spurious correlation: A correlation between two variables that does not arise because one causes the other — it may be produced by a third, shared factor or occur purely by chance.

findings.claim: always give both the direction (positive or negative) and the tail location (“the tail stretches to the right”) — one without the other rarely scores full marks
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about mark allocation/examiner behaviour. The Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 specification sets no rule that a skew description missing one element loses full marks, and no published Edexcel document states this. Under the invented-examiner-claims rule this must be reframed as advice, not as a statement about how marks are awarded.
findings.correction: When a question asks you to “describe” skew, give both the direction (positive or negative) and the tail location (“the tail stretches to the right”), so your description is complete.

findings.claim: examiners cannot award method marks for an answer with no working shown
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour. Nothing in the Edexcel GCSE Statistics 1ST0 specification states this; it is a claim about marking practice presented as fact.
findings.correction: For “show that” questions on the skewness formula, write out every step of the substitution so your method is fully visible.

findings.claim: On outlier questions, always state the effect on the mean compared with the median — this is usually a separate mark from simply naming the outlier.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are split within outlier questions; the specification does not state any such per-point mark allocation, so presenting it as typical marking practice is a fabrication.
findings.correction: On outlier questions, as well as naming the outlier, state its effect on the mean compared with the median, as questions often ask for both.

findings.claim: $$\text{standardised birth rate} = \frac{\text{crude rate}}{1000} \times \text{standard population}$$
findings.problem: This is not the standardised rate formula and does not standardise anything — applying the single overall crude rate to a standard population simply rescales the crude rate and cannot correct for age structure, which is the whole purpose of the measure. In Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 (and every standard treatment), standardisation applies each AGE-SPECIFIC rate to the corresponding age group of a standard population (given per 1,000) and sums the results. A student using the printed formula would score zero on a standardised-rate question.
findings.correction: $$\text{standardised birth rate} = \sum \left( \frac{\text{age-specific birth rate}}{1000} \times \text{standard population in that age group} \right)$$ where the standard population is given as a number per 1,000. Work out the expected births for each age group of the standard population, then add them to give the standardised rate per 1,000.

findings.claim: Foundation tier only requires the 4-point moving average, but Higher tier expects you to choose an appropriate number of points to match the cycle in the data.
findings.problem: Invented tier split. Moving averages are common content in Edexcel 1ST0 and Foundation-tier candidates are routinely asked for 3-point, 4-point or other n-point moving averages chosen to match the cycle in the data; there is no specification statement restricting Foundation tier to 4-point averages. A Foundation student told this may skip a question they are expected to answer.
findings.correction: Moving averages are assessed at both Foundation and Higher tier. Whatever tier you sit, choose the number of points to match the cycle in the data: quarterly data that repeats yearly needs a 4-point average, daily sales on a weekly cycle need a 7-point average, and data repeating every three periods needs a 3-point average.

findings.claim: a business owner looking at a steep upward trend line knows growth is accelerating, not just happening
findings.problem: Conceptually wrong and mark-affecting in 'Comment On'/'Describe' questions. The gradient of a straight trend line measures the RATE of change, not acceleration; a steep straight line shows fast but steady growth. Growth is only accelerating if the gradient itself is increasing (the trend curves upwards).
findings.correction: a business owner looking at a steep upward trend line knows the quantity is rising quickly; growth is only accelerating if the trend line becomes steeper over time

findings.claim: For population statistics, Edexcel uses the crude birth rate. The formula is always given in the exam:
findings.problem: Unevidenced exam claim. The Edexcel 1ST0 specification does not guarantee that the crude rate (or the standardised rate, where the same claim is repeated at n38) will be printed in every question; candidates are expected to know and be able to apply these rates. Telling students the formula will always appear discourages them from learning it.
findings.correction: For population statistics, Edexcel uses the crude birth rate. Learn this formula — it may not be given to you in the question:

findings.claim: All rate-of-change and index formulae you need will be given in the question — read them carefully rather than guessing from memory.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about exam presentation. Edexcel 1ST0 does not state that index number, percentage change or rate formulae are supplied in every question; some questions provide a formula, many do not. Students who rely on this may arrive unable to recall the index number or crude rate formula.
findings.correction: Learn the index number, percentage change and crude rate formulae — some questions supply a formula, but you cannot rely on it. Where a formula is given, substitute into it carefully rather than working from memory.

findings.claim: an answer-only response scores zero marks even if the final number is correct
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about marking. Edexcel mark schemes for 'Show That' questions award method marks for the working, and a correct answer with no working will normally lose the method marks — but there is no published Edexcel statement that such a response always scores zero across the board.
findings.correction: a 'Show That' question is marked on the working, so an answer with no substitution shown will lose the method marks even if the final number is right

findings.claim: GDP (Gross Domestic Product): tracks the total economic output of a country over time.
findings.problem: Slight imprecision in a list introduced as 'three named indices'. GDP is a measure of total economic output, not itself an index number; it becomes an index when expressed relative to a base year set at 100 (as the lesson's own knowledge check assumes).
findings.correction: GDP (Gross Domestic Product): the total economic output of a country, which is often expressed as an index relative to a base year set at 100 so that output can be compared over time.

findings.claim: it is the Bank of England’s inflation target
findings.problem: Imprecise attribution: the 2% inflation target is set by the Government (the Chancellor/HM Treasury) and is measured using CPI; the Bank of England is the body required to meet it.
findings.correction: it is the measure used for the Government’s 2% inflation target, which the Bank of England is required to meet

findings.claim: standardised birth rate — A birth rate adjusted so that two populations with different age structures can be compared fairly, calculated from the crude rate and a standard population figure.
findings.problem: The second half repeats the incorrect method from n39: a standardised rate is not calculated from the single overall crude rate, but by applying each age-specific rate to the matching age group of a standard population and summing.
findings.correction: standardised birth rate — A birth rate adjusted so that populations with different age structures can be compared fairly, found by applying each age-specific birth rate to the corresponding age group of a standard population (given per 1,000) and adding the results.

findings.claim: The specific investigation, data and methods your class used in coursework or a class project will be different
findings.problem: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 is 100% externally examined — two written papers, no coursework or controlled-assessment component. Referring to 'coursework' implies an assessed component that does not exist on this specification.
findings.correction: The specific investigation, data and methods your class used in a class project or practical investigation will be different

findings.claim: Both of your exam papers include an extended question that tests your ability to move across every stage, not just recall one technique in isolation.
findings.problem: The 1ST0 specification states only that each paper 'contains short response, medium response and extended response questions' and that questions cover 'the component parts of the statistical enquiry cycle'. It does not state that each paper contains one extended question, nor that such a question covers every stage. The related Key Fact claim that these questions come 'at the end of each paper' is also not stated anywhere in the specification.
findings.correction: Both of your exam papers contain short, medium and extended response questions, and questions can draw on the component parts of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle rather than one technique in isolation. (Key Fact: 'Extended response questions can draw on more than one of these stages at once.')

findings.claim: Recognising these errors — and explaining exactly how they distort the reader’s impression of the data — is a skill examiners test directly.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour/exam frequency. The specification requires students to recognise misleading diagrams, but no published Pearson document says examiners 'test this directly'.
findings.correction: Recognising these errors — and explaining exactly how they distort the reader’s impression of the data — is part of the specification content on misleading and misrepresentative diagrams.

findings.claim: This is why ‘increase the sample size’ is one of the most commonly credited improvements in evaluation questions, provided it is linked to a specific weakness rather than offered as a generic fix.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are awarded/what is commonly credited; no Pearson specification or published examiner report states this.
findings.correction: This is why increasing the sample size is a useful improvement to suggest — but only when it is linked to a specific weakness rather than offered as a generic fix.

findings.claim: using the wrong formula, or plotting frequency straight from a table with unequal class widths, is treated by the specification as a graphical misrepresentation in its own right, not just a calculation slip
findings.problem: Invented attribution to the specification. The 1ST0 specification requires frequency density for histograms with unequal class widths and separately lists misleading/misrepresentative diagrams; it does not classify plotting raw frequency as a 'graphical misrepresentation in its own right'.
findings.correction: For unequal-width histograms, frequency density (frequency ÷ class width) must be plotted on the vertical axis rather than raw frequency — plotting raw frequency produces a diagram whose bar heights give a false impression of the distribution.

findings.claim: Every evaluation point needs all three parts — weakness, impact, fix. Missing any one of them caps the mark in the Developing band, even if the statistics elsewhere in the answer are flawless.
findings.problem: Invented mark-band rule. Pearson's mark schemes for extended-response statistics questions do not contain a 'Developing band', and the specification states no rule that omitting one element caps a response at a named band. (The same problem applies to 'cannot reach the top mark band' in the 8-mark walkthrough.)
findings.correction: Every strong evaluation point has all three parts — weakness, impact, fix. An answer that omits the impact or the improvement is describing rather than evaluating, and will earn fewer marks even if the statistics elsewhere in the answer are flawless.

findings.claim: Stage 3 — Processing and Presenting Data
findings.problem: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle stage is named 'processing and representing data' in the specification wording (and topic 2 is 'Processing, representing and analysing data'). 'Presenting' is a paraphrase of the official stage name used consistently through the lesson, knowledge checks and glossary.
findings.correction: Stage 3 — Processing and Representing Data (update the stage name consistently in the Key Fact, glossary definition, matching task and Key Takeaways)

findings.claim: {"q": "What are the three parts of a full-mark evaluation point?", "a": "Identify the weakness, explain its impact, suggest an improvement."}
findings.problem: Flashcard rule breach: the answer is a list of three items, which should be split into separate cards; 'full-mark' also asserts an exam rule the specification does not state.
findings.correction: {"q": "After naming a weakness in an investigation, what must you explain about it?", "a": "Why it undermines the conclusion that was drawn."} (and add a second card: {"q": "What should every evaluation point end with?", "a": "A specific, workable improvement to the method."})

findings.claim: (parse failure)
findings.problem: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 1926 (char 1925)

findings.claim: On questions about explanatory and response variables, always state which axis each goes on — this earns marks even if you have misidentified which variable is which.
findings.problem: Invented mark-scheme claim. Nothing in the Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 specification (Issue 2) or its published mark schemes awards credit for naming axes on a question that asks candidates to identify the explanatory and response variables; marks on such items are for correct identification only (spec point 1b.03: explanatory (independent) variable should be on the 'x' axis is knowledge content, not a compensatory mark). Telling students an incorrect answer still scores is misleading.
findings.correction: On questions about explanatory and response variables, identify each variable clearly, and remember that the explanatory (independent) variable belongs on the horizontal axis and the response (dependent) variable on the vertical axis when you are asked to plot or comment on a scatter diagram.

findings.claim: Examiners are testing whether you know the specific term. On ‘Explain’ questions, a common error is saying “discrete data has whole numbers”
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertions about examiner intent and about what candidates commonly get wrong; no Edexcel 1ST0 specification or examiner report is cited and none is quoted as saying this. Claims about examiner behaviour or error frequency should not be presented as fact.
findings.correction: Be precise with terminology: write “discrete” or “continuous” rather than just “numerical”. On ‘Explain’ questions, avoid defining discrete data as “whole numbers only” — that is often true but not the definition, since UK shoe sizes are discrete yet include halves. The definition is that discrete data can only take specific, separate values.

findings.claim: A survey of 250 commuters grouped journey times into 12 class intervals of 5 minutes each, from 0-5 minutes up to 55-60 minutes.
findings.problem: Journey time is continuous, so intervals written as 0-5, 5-10, … 55-60 overlap at their boundaries, which contradicts the lesson's own rule (n18: class intervals must not overlap) and the model answer's requirement for 'non-overlapping' intervals. The arithmetic (12 × 5 minutes = 60) is correct; only the boundary notation is at fault.
findings.correction: A survey of 250 commuters grouped journey times into 12 class intervals of 5 minutes each, from 0 ≤ t < 5 minutes up to 55 ≤ t < 60 minutes. Several intervals contain fewer than 4 responses. Suggest an improved set of class intervals for this data, and justify your choice with reference to the problems with the original intervals. (Model answer: e.g. six intervals of the form 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20, … 50 ≤ t < 60.)

findings.claim: Writing “questionnaires are not always reliable” earns nothing — say why this questionnaire on this topic could produce inconsistent or inaccurate results
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how answers are marked. No Pearson Edexcel 1ST0 document states that a generic reliability comment scores zero; mark schemes for 'Explain' items credit valid points, and the degree of contextualisation required varies by question. Claims about what 'earns nothing' should not be presented as fact.
findings.correction: Writing “questionnaires are not always reliable” is too general to develop into a full answer — say why this questionnaire on this topic could produce inconsistent or inaccurate results, and whether sensitivity of the topic is driving it.

findings.claim: vague description of what was done, without evaluation, will not reach the top marks
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour/level descriptors. The specification requires critique of the statistical enquiry cycle, but no published Edexcel document is cited for this statement about top-band access, so it should be worded as guidance rather than as a rule about marking.
findings.correction: the question asks you to critique, so make sure you evaluate rather than simply describe what the investigator did.

findings.claim: Students frequently write “the data is reliable and valid” as if the two words mean the same thing, or swap one for the other. Used imprecisely, this costs marks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about candidate frequency and mark loss; no Edexcel 1ST0 examiner report or specification statement is cited to support either 'frequently' or 'costs marks'.
findings.correction: It is easy to write “the data is reliable and valid” as if the two words mean the same thing, or to swap one for the other. The two terms have distinct meanings and should be used precisely.

findings.claim: Bodies such as the Office for National Statistics (ONS), NHS Digital and the Met Office all publish large, high-quality datasets
findings.problem: NHS Digital ceased to exist as a separate organisation when it merged into NHS England in February 2023; naming it as a current publisher of datasets is out of date for a lesson targeting the summer 2027 series.
findings.correction: Bodies such as the Office for National Statistics (ONS), NHS England and the Met Office all publish large, high-quality datasets

findings.claim: A laboratory experiment removes outside influences (high control).
findings.problem: Overstatement: a laboratory setting controls or reduces the influence of extraneous variables but cannot remove them entirely; the specification content is about the level of control, not total elimination.
findings.correction: A laboratory experiment controls outside influences as far as possible (high control).

findings.claim: You are not expected to physically carry out a random selection using these tools in the exam — you need to understand how each one produces a fair, unbiased choice.
findings.problem: This contradicts the Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Statistics 1ST0 specification content on data collection, which requires students to be able to obtain/select a simple random sample using random numbers (random number tables, generators, calculator functions); Edexcel papers regularly ask candidates to describe or carry out the selection process (e.g. 'Describe how she could use random numbers to select a sample of 20 from the 200 students'). Telling students the skill is not assessed removes a genuinely examinable technique from their revision.
findings.correction: Random selection can be carried out using dice, shuffled cards, printed random number lists, or the random number function on a calculator. You may be asked in the exam to describe how to use random numbers to select a sample — for example, number every member of the sampling frame, then read numbers in order, ignoring repeats and numbers out of range, until you have enough people.

findings.claim: Calling stratification itself “a sampling method” is a common error that loses marks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour and about how marks are awarded. No Edexcel 1ST0 specification statement or published mark scheme says marks are lost for this; Edexcel's own specification and mark schemes routinely use the term 'stratified sampling' / 'stratified sample' as a sampling method. The conceptual point (stratify first, then sample randomly within strata) is sound, but the mark claim is not.
findings.correction: Stratification divides the population into subgroups before sampling begins. Random sampling is then the method actually used within each stratum — which is why the full method is called stratified random sampling. Make sure your answers show both steps.

findings.claim: On ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about sampling, examiners want you to name a specific weakness in the method described — not just say ‘it could be biased’.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about what examiners want. The advice itself is reasonable, but it should be framed as what the question command word requires, not as a claim about examiner preferences, which no published Edexcel document states.
findings.correction: On ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about sampling, a justification needs a specific weakness in the method described — not just ‘it could be biased’. State which group would be over- or under-represented and why, then suggest a concrete alternative.

findings.claim: Never describe stratification itself as ‘a sampling method’ — it is the step taken before sampling, and marks are lost for blurring the two.
findings.problem: Invented mark-scheme claim. Edexcel 1ST0 materials use 'stratified sampling' as the name of a sampling method, and no published Edexcel mark scheme penalises candidates for that wording. Students following this advice may avoid the board's own terminology.
findings.correction: Be precise about the two steps: the population is stratified (divided into proportional subgroups) first, and random sampling is then used within each stratum — together this is stratified random sampling.

findings.claim: It looks organised because it is proportional to subgroup sizes, but because selection within each quota is not random, it carries the same bias risk as opportunity sampling.
findings.problem: Misleading: quota sampling means a fixed target number is set for each subgroup; those quotas need not be proportional to the subgroup sizes in the population (the lesson's own example of 30 + 30 women is an equal, not proportional, quota). Proportionality is the defining feature of stratified sampling, not quota sampling.
findings.correction: The quotas may or may not reflect the actual proportions in the population, and because selection within each quota is not random, it carries the same bias risk as opportunity sampling.

findings.claim: Quota: Proportional to subgroup sizes, but not random within each quota, so it shares opportunity sampling’s bias risk.
findings.problem: Same imprecision as above: quotas are fixed target numbers per subgroup and are not necessarily proportional to population subgroup sizes.
findings.correction: Quota: Sets a fixed target for each subgroup (not necessarily proportional to the population), but selection within each quota is not random, so it shares opportunity sampling’s bias risk.

findings.claim: cluster sampling: Sampling where the population is divided into naturally occurring groups (clusters), and entire clusters are selected rather than individuals.
findings.problem: Incomplete: in cluster sampling the clusters themselves are selected at random. Omitting the random selection of clusters loses the feature that distinguishes it from simply choosing a convenient group, which is the point an 'Explain'/'Comment On' answer needs.
findings.correction: cluster sampling: Sampling where the population is divided into naturally occurring groups (clusters), a number of whole clusters are then chosen at random, and everyone in those clusters forms the sample.

findings.claim: Before sampling can begin, you need a <dfn class="term" data-def="A list of population members available for sampling.">sample frame</dfn>
findings.problem: Terminology: Edexcel 1ST0 specification and papers use the term 'sampling frame'. 'Sample frame' is understood but is not the board's wording, and consistency helps students recognise the term in question stems.
findings.correction: Before sampling can begin, you need a <dfn class="term" data-def="A list of population members available for sampling.">sampling frame</dfn> (use 'sampling frame' consistently throughout the lesson and glossary)

findings.claim: because the researcher knows roughly half will be forced to say “yes”, the true proportion answering honestly can still be estimated for the whole group
findings.problem: Misstates what the random response method estimates. The design fixes the proportion answering honestly at roughly 50% (it is known, not estimated); what is estimated from the excess of 'yes' answers over the expected forced 'yes' count is the proportion of the group who actually have the sensitive characteristic. Edexcel-style random response questions require students to subtract the forced 'yes' responses and then scale up to estimate the proportion with the behaviour, so this wording could lead a student to describe the wrong quantity.
findings.correction: because the researcher knows roughly half will be forced to say “yes”, those forced “yes” answers can be subtracted from the total, and the remainder scaled up to estimate the proportion of the whole group who really do the sensitive behaviour.

findings.claim: a vague answer such as “make the question clearer” scores little. ... show the row or column addition explicitly so the examiner can see exactly where the error lies
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertions about examiner behaviour and marking outcomes; no Pearson Edexcel GCSE Statistics (1ST0) specification or published board document states that such answers 'score little' or describes what the examiner is looking for in these terms.
findings.correction: On ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about questionnaire design, answer in two parts: name the exact fault (“this is a leading question because it implies exercising less is wrong”) and then give a specific fix (“rewrite as a neutral question with no implied preferred answer”). For data-cleaning questions with a table, write out the row or column addition in full so your working shows where the error lies. For Higher-tier questions on control groups or the random response technique, link your answer back to reducing bias or protecting anonymity rather than only describing the method.

findings.claim: "sample frame"
findings.problem: Incorrect terminology in a distractor option; the Edexcel GCSE Statistics specification uses the term 'sampling frame'.
findings.correction: "sampling frame"

findings.claim: Estimating how long the questionnaire takes, so respondents know what to expect.
findings.problem: Misstates the statistical purpose of timing a pilot. The reason for timing is to check the questionnaire is not so long that it lowers response rates or produces rushed, unreliable answers, not simply to inform respondents.
findings.correction: Estimating how long the questionnaire takes, so it can be shortened if its length would reduce the response rate or cause rushed answers.
